definition: A training objective where random tokens in a sequence are hidden and the model learns to predict them from surrounding context.
details: Masked language modeling, used to train BERT, encourages bidirectional understanding of context, in contrast to the left-to-right prediction used by autoregressive models.

explainer.lead: Masked language modeling is a training objective where random tokens in a sequence are hidden and the model predicts them from surrounding context. It matters because it forces bidirectional understanding of context.

tiers.eli5: It's a fill-in-the-blank exercise: hide some words in a sentence and have the model guess them from what's left on both sides.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use it to train models such as BERT, which read context in both directions. A pitfall is that hiding tokens creates a train–test mismatch, since real inputs never contain intentional blanks.
tiers.paperLevel: Random tokens in a sequence are masked and the model learns to predict them from the surrounding context. This differs from the left-to-right prediction of autoregressive models by encouraging bidirectional context.

explainer.example: In 'the cat sat on the ___', the final token is hidden and the model learns to predict 'mat' from both preceding and following context.

citation.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
